title: Generations, Small Object Heap, and Large Object Heap (SOH and LOH)
hook: The garbage collector divides the managed heap into generations so short-lived objects die fast. The Small Object Heap (SOH) holds most objects; the Large Object Heap (LOH) holds allocations roughly 85,000 bytes and larger.

blocks.text: Generation 0 is a nursery for brand-new allocations. Objects that survive a collection are promoted to generation 1, then generation 2. The SOH is collected frequently and compacted. The LOH stores large arrays and strings; it is collected with generation 2 and historically fragments because it is not compacted every collection.

entries.plainDefinition: Heap region for objects under the large-object threshold.
entries.example: A List<int> with ten items lives on the SOH.

entries.plainDefinition: Heap region for allocations at or above ~85,000 bytes.
entries.example: A 90 KB byte[] for a CSV row buffer lands on the LOH.

entries.plainDefinition: Moving a surviving object to an older generation.
entries.example: A singleton cache entry promoted to gen 2 stays until a full collection.

blocks.text: Most allocations die young. Nursery collections are cheap. A service that allocates one giant buffer per request pays generation-2 and LOH costs instead of quick gen-0 reclaims. Understanding SOH versus LOH explains why pooling and streaming matter for CSV imports and image buffers.

blocks.title: LOH threshold rule of thumb
blocks.body: Arrays and strings at or above ~85,000 bytes go to the LOH. Prefer ArrayPool<byte>, chunking, or streaming when you do not need one contiguous giant buffer.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Allocate in gen 0
items.body: new bumps a pointer in the nursery — very fast.

items.title: Survive a collection
items.body: Live objects are marked and promoted to gen 1.

items.title: Survive again
items.body: Promoted to gen 2 — collected less often, more expensive.

items.title: Large allocation
items.body: Size at threshold skips nursery semantics and lands on LOH.

diagram.title: Generations and heaps
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  A[new object] --> B[Gen 0 SOH]
  B -->|survives| C[Gen 1 SOH]
  C -->|survives| D[Gen 2 SOH]
  E[large array 85KB+] --> F[LOH]
  F -->|collected with| D

snippet.label: Small vs large allocation
snippet.code:
var small = new byte[1024];       // SOH, gen 0
var large = new byte[90_000];     // LOH
Console.WriteLine(GC.GetGeneration(small)); // often 0
Console.WriteLine(GC.GetGeneration(large)); // 2 for LOH objects
snippet.explanation: Size determines heap segment. LOH objects start in generation 2.

snippet.label: ArrayPool instead of LOH churn
snippet.explanation: Renting reuses arrays instead of allocating a new LOH object every request.

snippet.label: Check LOH compaction mode
snippet.explanation: Modern .NET can compact LOH on demand or when a heap hard limit is hit.

blocks.title: Generational GC contrast
rows: Different heuristics; no identical LOH knob

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming every new byte[] is gen 0 — large arrays skip to LOH. Holding references to gen-2 caches that pin old graphs alive. Ignoring LOH fragmentation in long-running imports.

interviewTakeaways: Gen 0 is a nursery; promotion means the object lived through a collection.
LOH is ~85 KB+; collected with gen 2; fragmentation is the risk.
Pool or stream large buffers instead of per-request LOH allocations.
commonPitfalls: Treating a 100 KB buffer like a cheap gen-0 allocation.
Never returning rented arrays to ArrayPool.
Assuming LOH is compacted every GC.

jsTsCorrelations.note: V8 is generational too, but you do not tune an LOH threshold the same way. Large TypedArrays still live in the JS heap.
